fixes.explanation: Tarshish it is, friend. Jonah says that's where he was so quick to flee (Jonah 4:2). He says it right in his prayer to the LORD, which takes some nerve.
Damascus is a real city, friend, but it's not in Jonah's prayer. He says he was so quick to flee toward Tarshish (Jonah 4:2). I'd have asked somebody for directions, and I'd have been lost anyway.

That's the one, baker. Jonah says he knew God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, One who relents from sending disaster (Jonah 4:2). So the reason he gives for running is who God is. He says it right out loud to the LORD, and honestly, I love him for the honesty.

Nice try, friend, but the text doesn't mention the road at all. Jonah says he knew God is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and One who relents from sending disaster (Jonah 4:2). That's his reason, in his own words. A long walk I could understand, but that isn't the reason Jonah gives.

Careful, friend, that's not what he asks. Jonah says, “…please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.” (Jonah 4:3). He asks for his own life to end, and nothing about Nineveh in that request. I think this one is heavy, so I'll just say the LORD answers him next (Jonah 4:4).

Yes, baker, that's the question. “Have you any right to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4). Jonah asks to die and the LORD answers with a question, a short one. I wish I could answer my own grumpy days with a question like that.
It's a clever guess, friend, but that question isn't in the text. The LORD replies, “Have you any right to be angry?” (Jonah 4:4). One short question is all He says in that verse.

It's true, friend, though I see why it sounds odd. The text says Jonah made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to see what would happen to the city (Jonah 4:5). So he sat there on purpose, watching Nineveh. I'd have brought cookies, but that's me.

A vine, baker! The LORD God appointed a vine, and it grew up to provide shade over Jonah's head to ease his discomfort (Jonah 4:6). Jonah already had a shelter, and now he had a vine over his head too. That's shade with a bonus.
True, baker. The text says Jonah “…was greatly pleased with the plant.” (Jonah 4:6). A little shade will do that to a person. I've been pleased with less.

Not false, friend. Jonah “…was greatly pleased with the plant.” (Jonah 4:6). He was angry earlier in the chapter, and now he's delighted with a plant. I think a little shade can turn a lot of moods around.
A worm, baker. When dawn came the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered (Jonah 4:7). A worm took down the plant. I've lost a whole batch to less, believe me.

A goat would work fast on a vine, friend, I'll give you that. But the text says God appointed a worm that attacked the plant so that it withered (Jonah 4:7). The worm did the job, and no goat was needed.

Right, baker, it's false. Jonah grows faint and says, “…it is better for me to die than to live.” (Jonah 4:8). There's no admission about Nineveh here. The sun was beating on his head, and what he says is about himself, not Nineveh.
